source.title: Consistency Training Helps Stop Sycophancy and Jailbreaks
source.authors: A. Irpan; Alexander Matt Turner; Mark Kurzeja; David K. Elson; Rohin Shah

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Reports jailbreak attack-success rates for attacked prompts, bearing on whether jailbreaks can overcome refusal; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or per-token KL methods.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates jailbreak prompts that include varied wrappers, including prefixes and suffixes in its training-data construction, and reports attack-success rates. It does not report rates by specific attack technique, compliant-start prefills, or decoding change. Sycophancy results and capability scores do not measure the claim versions here. No results are reported for harmful or ordinary-benign fine-tuning as a safety-eroding intervention, first-token KL concentration, or safety localization in weights.
record.test_reason: A jailbreak-mitigation study (BCT/ACT consistency training vs DPO and stale SFT). It cites the shallow-alignment hypothesis as motivation and future work but does not test it. Its control ASRs come from mixed wrapper jailbreaks (mostly roleplay, plus prefixes/suffixes and list-hiding), aggregated without isolating opening-position bypasses. There are no prefill, decoding, per-token KL, fine-tuning-attack or depth measures.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with additions. The authors conclude that consistency training (BCT on outputs, ACT on residual activations) reduces sycophancy and jailbreaks. BCT and ACT are equal on sycophancy; BCT cuts jailbreak ASR more, while ACT has virtually no cost to benign refusals. Self-generated data avoids specification and capability staleness, though evidence on capability staleness was mixed for jailbreaks.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains paired-prompt output or activation consistency (BCT/ACT), rather than testing harmful-example fine-tuning, benign instruction fine-tuning, or per-token KL concentration.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model, training method, and evaluation set. BCT generally reduces ASR more than ACT; ACT remains much less effective on ClearHarm for Gemma 3 models than BCT.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety-trained Gemma 2/3 and Gemini 2.5 Flash comply with mixed wrapper jailbreaks (roleplay, prefixes/suffixes, list-hiding) at 39–89% ASR on ClearHarm/WildguardTest before mitigation (Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generic prompt-wrapper jailbreaks defeat refusal in current safety-trained models, independent of opening-position mechanisms.

record.problems: The jailbreak ASR evaluations aggregate across attack types; no result isolates prefilling, suffixes, or decoding changes. The prompted Gemini 2.5 Flash judge agreed with the authors' labels 91% for is-unsafe and 79% for refused-benign on the sampled checks.
record.rows_left_out: No ASR rows left out. Other reported measures, including sycophancy avoidance, benign-answer rates, and MMLU accuracy, do not directly measure the claim versions tested here.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, isolated suffix or decoding attacks. Jailbreak ASR aggregates mixed wrapper attacks.
No weight or rank localization. The ACT last-half-layers ablation concerns sycophancy only.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow.
BCT/ACT are not depth-spreading methods and no token-depth robustness is measured. Qi et al.'s augmentation is mentioned only as future work.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'tests' link is not justified. The shallow-alignment hypothesis is only cited in related work and future work. The mitigation rows are method comparisons. Training data were filtered to prompts refused clean but answered when wrapped; the eval mixes seen and unseen jailbreaks. The judge is prompted Gemini 2.5 Flash (91%/79% agreement on hard samples).

versions.untested_parts: Whether a few to a few hundred harmful fine-tuning examples remove refusal.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction data raises harmful compliance.
Per-token KL by response position and whether divergence is concentrated in early tokens.
The reported ASR aggregates across attacks; the paper does not isolate compliant-start prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes in the evaluation results.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Whether safety training spreads safety beyond early response tokens and whether such deepening holds up.

relation.reason: Section 2 discusses shallow safety alignment as motivation; Section 6 proposes combining consistency training with Qi et al.'s augmentation. Neither tests nor implements that finding.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates consistency training against aggregated wrapper jailbreaks without isolating opening-token bypass or testing safety depth. Deepening via randomly positioned refusals is proposed only as future work.

source_check.notes: All sampled values and confidence intervals match. The reported ASRs measure aggregate jailbreak vulnerability, not a specific shallow-alignment mechanism; cannot_determine and no version verdicts are appropriate.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Control models on ClearHarm and WildguardTest
reader_labels.reason: Control ASRs show jailbreak success in the evaluated prompt sets (r01, r05, r09, r13, r17, r22, r27, r32, r37, r42). This supports jailbreak vulnerability in these tested settings, not the specific first-token explanation.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Fine-tuned models and aggregate ACT/BCT results
reader_labels.reason: ACT, BCT, DPO, and stale-data SFT often substantially lower ASR, although rates remain nonzero and ACT is less effective in some settings (r02-r04, r06-r08, r10-r12, r14-r16, r18-r21, r23-r26, r28-r31, r33-r36, r38-r41, r43-r49). The paper does not isolate the specific bypass mechanisms.
